In this section of *Sitting in the Buddha’s Waiting Room*, the teaching focuses on direct observation of the mind: *"All of his teachings point to the true source of inner strength and security: selfless just-knowing awareness."* The central guidance is to step back from the habitual impulse to control or fix present experience, and instead cultivate a spacious, non-reactive presence. When we investigate thoughts and feelings without identification (*anattā*), their grip on the heart naturally dissolves. It is like It is like a small boat floating on a calm mountain lake beneath an open sky. Rest in that clear, unentangled knowing.

In 'Sitting in the Buddha’s Waiting Room' (Sitting in the Buddha’s Waiting Room), how should a meditator handle restless thoughts and mental chatter?

The text reflects: *"The image that came to my mind and which I shared with her was one of our sitting in the Buddha’s waiting room."* Thoughts are merely passing mental formations (*saṅkhāra*); they have no solid core unless we feed them with belief. When a thought arises, simply recognize it as 'thinking, thinking' without jumping into the storyline. It is like It is like an anchor dropped deep into the seabed, keeping the boat steady in stormy waves. Be the vast, open sky through which thoughts pass like harmless clouds.

What practical guidance on meditation and body awareness is given in 'Sitting in the Buddha’s Waiting Room' (Sitting in the Buddha’s Waiting Room)?

The teaching highlights: *"To use another metaphor: when we are swimming in the ocean and roll over onto our back and float, it is not the fact we believe that floating is possible that prevents us from sinking; it is a whole body-mind effort."* Working with the breath and physical sensations grounds the mind in the immediate present (*paccuppanna*). Do not force or manipulate the breath; simply maintain relaxed, continuous mindfulness of each in-and-out cycle. It is like It is like a bird gliding through open space without needing to build a nest on a cloud. Let the body settle and the heart become still.
